Content:
Recall that the conditional statement and its contrapositive are logically equivalent.

Content:
[MATH: P \Rightarrow Q \equiv \neg Q \Rightarrow \neg P]

Content:
We can use the contrapositive to prove statements about divisibility. To demonstrate, let's prove the following proposition using the contrapositive:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{d \not\mid 72}_{P}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{d \not\mid 8}_{Q}.]

Content:
The contrapositive form of this statement is
[MATH: \underbrace{\lnot \Big( d \not\mid 8 \Big)}_{\lnot \, Q}
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\underbrace{\lnot \Big( d \not\mid 72 \Big)}_{\lnot \, P},]
which is equivalent to
[MATH: d \mid 8 \quad\Rightarrow\quad d \mid 72.]
So, we proceed as follows:

Content:
> The contrapositive of the statement is
> [MATH: d \mid 8 \quad\Rightarrow\quad d \mid 72.]
> We will prove this statement instead of the original one.

Content:
Recall that if an integer [MATH: a] is divisible by [MATH: d,] then there exists an integer [MATH: k] such that [MATH: a = d \cdot k.]

Content:
Using this definition, we continue our proof as follows:

Content:
> By the definition of integer divisibility, we have
> [MATH: d \mid 8
> \qquad\Leftrightarrow\qquad
> 8 = d \cdot k]
> for some integer [MATH: k.]

Content:
Since we need to consider divisors of [MATH: 72] instead of [MATH: 8,] we multiply the last equation by [MATH: 9{:}]

Content:
> Multiplying both sides of [MATH: 8 = d k] by [MATH: 9,] we obtain
> [MATH: 9 ⋅ 8|= 9 ⋅ dk; 72|= 9dk; 72|= d(9k); 72|= dm]
> where [MATH: m = 9k] is an integer.

Content:
Finally, we use the definition of integer divisibility once more:

Content:
> Therefore, by the definition of integer divisibility, [MATH: 72 = dm] means that [MATH: d \mid 72.]

Content:
For clarity, let's restate the proposition and its proof.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

> Therefore, by the definition of integer divisibility, [MATH: 72 = dm] means that [MATH: d \mid 72.]
